name: Sanggau
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Only comparative refs (Smith 2017 Borneo classification); no grammar or phonology of Sanggau located

new_statements.quote: From a historical point of view, the existence of a full/reduced vowel distinction in the penultimate syllable is unexpected for two reasons: 1) the modern Land Dayak languages are stress-final, a pattern which is likely reconstructable to the proto-language. It is typologically unexpected for unstressed vowels to have a greater number of distinctions than stressed vowels. [fn. 2, p. 112:] Southern Land Dayak includes Golik, Kembayan, Jangkang, Ribun, and Sanggau, among others. [Smith 2017: 185:] Most importantly, stress in many of the languages of West Kalimantan is consistently word-final, a feature of most of the Land Dayak languages of the Kapuas River area.
new_statements.citation: Smith, Alexander D. 2019. A second look at Proto-Land Dayak vowels. Oceanic Linguistics 58(1): 110-142.
new_statements.locator: p. 111 (section 1, Introduction); fn. 2 on p. 112 lists Sanggau among Southern Land Dayak. Corroborated by Smith 2017 dissertation p. 185 (section 2.8.2).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable of the word; asserted for the Land Dayak subgroup as a whole (and for 'most' Land Dayak languages of the Kapuas River area, where Sanggau lies) by the one linguist who has collected first-hand Sanggau data, not stated for Sanggau individually.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned for Land Dayak/Sanggau (Smith 2017 raises secondary stress only for Merap, a Kayanic language).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Sanggau; Smith 2017 hedges with 'most of the Land Dayak languages of the Kapuas River area' and describes Hliboi Bidayuh as 'word-final and strong' with vowel breaking as a correlate.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, from elicited wordlist citation forms (Smith 2017 fieldwork, 200-item comparative lists); Sanggau transcriptions in Smith 2017 carry no stress marks. Group-level generalization, not a Sanggau-specific phonological description.
new_statements.identity_note: sang1339 / scg is the Land Dayak (Southern Land Dayak; Glottolog 'South Bidayuh') language of Sanggau regency on the Kapuas, with Ethnologue dialects Dosan, Mayau, Sanggau (very heterogeneous, possibly more than one language). It is NOT Sanggau Malay (Malayic), which the Indonesian Wikipedia article 'Bahasa Sanggau' wrongly Smith's Sanggau data (the only first-hand modern data found) come from one consultant 'in and around Sanggau' town. The stress statement is at the Land Dayak subgroup level (Smith 2019) / 'most of the Land Dayak languages of the Kapuas River area' (Smith 2017), not a Sanggau-specific description; sibling Hliboi Bidayuh (hlib1234?) is described individually as word-final.

sources.citation: Smith, Alexander D. 2017. The Languages of Borneo: A comprehensive classification. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa. 724 pp.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Contains Smith's own Sanggau fieldwork data (consultant Helmut, 'in and around Sanggau', p. 15) and a Land Dayak historical-phonology section (2.6, pp. 139-168) with Sanggau reflex tables, but no Sanggau-specific stress sentence. Group-level statement p. 185: 'stress in many of the languages of West Kalimantan is consistently word-final, a feature of most of the Land Dayak languages of the Kapuas River area.' p. 166: 'Stress in Hliboi Bidayuh is word-final and strong' (Hliboi, not Sanggau).
No descriptive references at all; classification Landak > Bidayuh > South Bidayuh; only Smith 2017 (pp. 139-168), Smith & Rama 2022 and Ethnologue cited.

sources.note: Dialects Dosan, Mayau, Sanggau; 'Very heterogenous dialects, probably more than 1 language'; population 45,000 (Wurm & Hattori 1981); no phonology.

sources.citation: Ray, Sidney H. 1913. The languages of Borneo. Sarawak Museum Journal 1(4): 1-196.
sources.note: 'Sangau' appears only as a column in the comparative vocabulary (second-hand Dutch-era lists, pp. 10-11 describe the Sanggau kingdom); the only stress remark in the whole work concerns Ngaju Mantangai sentence stress. Nothing on Sanggau stress.
English page: stub, Ethnologue-only reference. Indonesian page files Sanggau MALAY (Malayic) under code scg/sang1339 - an identity conflation; no phonology on either.
